copy: Home › Grooming problems
You’ve noticed something after a bath, a brush, a trim or a trip to the groomer, and you want to know whether it’s the grooming or something your vet should see.
By Grooming Dogs · Updated October 5, 2026
This page helps you work out what to change and when to call your vet. It can’t diagnose your dog. Only a vet who examines your dog can do that.
Short answer:
Stop the grooming task that seems to be causing the problem. Don’t push on to finish.
Some problems are linked to how a dog was groomed: leftover shampoo, a coat left damp, a hot or damaged clipper blade, or water in the ears [1] [2] [8] [11] . Changing the technique can help.
See your vet if your dog seems in pain, the problem is spreading or getting worse, there’s broken skin, swelling, discharge or bleeding that won’t stop, or your dog seems unwell in themselves.
When in doubt, call your vet. Several of these signs look alike, and some need prompt treatment [4] [8] .
Grooming can cause or expose problems, but the same sign can have many causes. Skin problems are one of the most common reasons owners take their pets to the vet [14] .
A grooming factor is more likely when all of these are true:
the problem is mild and appeared soon after a particular grooming task;
you can see a likely cause, such as shampoo you didn’t fully rinse out;
your dog seems otherwise comfortable and well;
it’s improving, not getting worse.
Even then, keep an eye on it and change what you do next time.
Contact your vet if any of these apply:
Pain: your dog seems sore, cries when touched, or won’t let you near the area.
Spreading: the problem is spreading or getting worse rather than better.
Broken skin: there’s a cut, sores, scabs, oozing or pus.
Swelling: for example, a puffy ear flap [3] .
Unwell: your dog is quiet, lethargic, or off their food. With skin changes after a bath, this needs prompt veterinary attention [4] [5] .
Not settling: the problem hasn’t settled, or keeps coming back.

Don’t treat it yourself. Don’t put home remedies, human creams or leftover medication on your dog’s skin, ears or eyes unless your vet tells you to. Your vet needs to find the cause before the right treatment is clear [7] [8] .

Itching after a bath:
Leftover shampoo can irritate the skin, which is why rinsing completely matters [1] .
Use only products made for dogs [1] .
If the itch started after a new product, stop using it and see whether the itch settles.
Redness after clipping:
Clipper blades can get hot during use [11] .
A damaged or broken blade can injure the skin [11] .
Holding the blade against the skin can irritate it, which is why blades should be kept away from the skin [13] .
If redness appears in the areas you clipped, it may be related to the clipping. Next time, check the blade and keep it off the skin. See clipping safely .
Scratching can make things worse: a red patch can turn into a raw, oozing, painful sore if your dog keeps scratching, licking or chewing it [8] .
See your vet, promptly, if:
the skin becomes painful, broken, scabbed or oozing;
bumps or sores appear and spread over the next day or so, especially along the back;
your dog seems quiet, unwell or off their food.

Vets recognize a serious skin infection that can develop within a day of a bath or grooming. It causes painful bumps, sores and crusts, often along the back. Affected dogs can become lethargic and stop eating, and it needs prompt veterinary treatment [4] [5] .
Some dogs shake their heads after a bath or a groom, and grooming can irritate an ear that’s already prone to problems [2] :
Water: water in the ear creates the moist conditions that can lead to infection, and a warm, wet, floppy ear covering the ear opening can keep it damp [2] .
Loose hair: hair clipped around the head can fall into the ear canal [2] .

What to change: dry the outer ear after bathing [1] , and keep water out of the ears during a bath. See rinsing and drying properly . How to clean the ear is covered in cleaning ears safely . Don’t push anything into the ear canal.
See your vet if:
Ear signs: you notice redness, swelling, discharge, a strong or yeasty smell, or pawing at the ears [1] [13] ;
Pain: the ear is painful to touch;
Persistent shaking: your dog keeps shaking or scratching after the ear has had time to dry;
Swollen ear flap: the ear flap swells and feels soft or fluid-filled. Hard shaking or scratching can break a small blood vessel in the ear flap, and that needs a vet [3] .
A smell soon after a bath often comes from moisture left behind:
Thick coats: a coat that stays wet holds moisture against the skin [8] .
Skin folds: dirt and bacteria in folds can cause irritation and infection, so dry them thoroughly [14] .
Mats: dense mats hold moisture against the skin, and infections can develop under them [12] . See brushing and mats .
What to change: dry your dog completely, including folds, ears and dense areas. See rinsing and drying properly .
See your vet if:
the smell comes from one place rather than the whole coat, such as the ears [13] , the mouth, or the rear end (especially with scooting or licking there) [13] ;
the smell comes with greasy, flaky, red or itchy skin [7] ;
the smell keeps coming back after your dog is fully dry.
A smell that bathing doesn’t fix isn’t a grooming problem. Don’t try to mask it with more frequent baths or perfumed products.
Dry, flaky skin has many possible causes, and bathing is only one of them [7] . On the grooming side, the factors to check are [7] :
harsh soaps or products not made for dogs;
not rinsing thoroughly, which can leave skin flaky.
What to change: use a shampoo made for dogs, and rinse until no product is left. See rinsing and drying properly . How often to bathe is covered in the grooming schedule .

Talk to your vet even if you think bathing is the cause, so other causes can be ruled out [7] . See your vet sooner if the flaking comes with itching, redness, hair loss, scabs, smell or greasy skin [7] .
Don’t treat dry skin with oils, human moisturizers or supplements unless your vet recommends them.
Reddish-brown staining below the eyes is common in some dogs, especially light-coated ones:
What causes it: it’s usually caused by the shape of the eyelids and face sending tears onto the fur instead of down the tear duct [9] .
Underlying eye problems: most dogs with tear stains don’t have one, but some do [9] .
What you can do:
Wipe gently: clean around the eyes, not in them, with a soft, damp cloth, and avoid rubbing across the eye [1] .
Dry the area afterward [9] .
Keep the hair around the eyes short: this helps. See trimming around the eyes .
Ask your vet first before putting any cleaning solution near your dog’s eyes [9] .
See your vet if:
your dog has new tear staining they didn’t have before [9] ;
there’s squinting, redness, cloudy or colored discharge, or your dog is pawing at an eye [1] ;
your dog is squinting or keeping an eye closed after a bath. Shampoo in the eye can cause painful damage to the surface of the eye [12] .
After a close clip, the coat usually grows back within a few months [10] . Sometimes it doesn’t. A veterinary dermatology handbook describes the following [10] :
3–4 months: in otherwise healthy dogs, the coat generally starts regrowing within this time, and failure to regrow within it is considered abnormal.
Which dogs: it can happen in any breed, but is seen more often in dogs with thick, plush coats.
How long: some dogs take a year or more to regrow fully.
Double coats: shaving one can also leave the undercoat and topcoat growing back unevenly [6] . See should you shave a double-coated dog .
See your vet if:
the coat hasn’t started growing back within about 3–4 months [10] ;
there’s new thinning or bald patches somewhere that wasn’t clipped;
there are skin changes or other health changes.
Other causes need to be ruled out, especially in middle-aged and older dogs [10] . For older dogs, see grooming an older dog .
Stop grooming straight away. Don’t try to finish the job. Keep your dog calm and somewhere safe, and look at the area without forcing your dog to let you handle it.
What to do next:
Nicked nail quick: follow the steps in if a nail bleeds . Call your vet if the bleeding doesn’t stop.
Cuts, sores or other injuries to the skin: contact your vet [1] . A cut from scissors can need stitches. Vets regularly see injuries from mats cut out at home [12] .
A burn from a dryer: contact your vet. Dryers held too close to the skin can burn [13] .
Limping, crying out, or not wanting to be touched somewhere after grooming: contact your vet.
Get veterinary help urgently, or go to an emergency vet if yours is closed, if your dog:
has bleeding that won’t stop;
has a deep or gaping wound;
is having trouble breathing;
collapses or seems very weak;
is in severe pain.
If it happened at a groomer:
First: get your dog checked by a vet.
Then: ask the groomer what happened, and keep any vet notes and photos.
Raising a concern: see if something goes wrong at the groomer .
If your dog is now frightened of grooming, see if your dog resists grooming . If the change is sudden and they also seem sore, see your vet first.
My dog has scabs after a haircut. Is that normal?
Scabs mean the skin was broken or irritated, so they’re worth a vet check rather than waiting:
Possible causes: a hot or damaged blade, a nick, or scratching at irritated skin [8] [11] .
Infection: less often, scabs and sores after grooming are a sign of a skin infection that needs prompt treatment [4] .
See your vet the same day if the scabs are spreading, painful, or your dog seems unwell.
Can I put coconut oil on my dog's dry skin?
Ask your vet before putting anything on your dog’s skin. Dry, flaky skin has many possible causes, and the right approach depends on the cause [7] .
Can I treat a hot spot at home?

No, see your vet. A hot spot is a painful, inflamed, often oozing patch that can spread quickly. Waiting for it to clear up on its own tends to make it worse, and your vet will need to find what’s causing the itching [8] .
